hook.line: Four players draw a tile and discard a tile, racing to make four sets and a pair. A game born in China grew its own way in Japan once it gained “riichi”.
hook.say: Hi, Peacotile here! Let’s follow the story of riichi mahjong together.

ch.t: From a Chinese port to the world
ch.say: The tile game took shape in a Chinese port town in the 19th century.
p: Mahjong is thought to have taken shape in the late 19th century, in the Qing era, on China’s eastern coast. Ningbo is known as its birthplace, and tiles from the 1870s still survive. Its name means “sparrow” in Chinese — some say because shuffling tiles sounds like sparrows chattering.

In 1920 Joseph P. Babcock, an American living in Shanghai, published rules in English, and mahjong became a craze in America. In Japan, mahjong parlours opened in Tokyo in the 1920s, and in 1929 the Japan Mahjong League was founded with the writer Kikuchi Kan as its president. After the war, “riichi” — declaring a ready hand — was added, and Japan’s own riichi mahjong was born.
st: Known as the birthplace; tiles from this time survive

ch.say: Four groups of three and a matching pair — that’s a win!
ch.cap: A winning hand: 1-2-3 characters · 4-5-6 dots · 2-3-4 bamboos · three Easts · two Red Dragons (the glowing pair)
p: Draw a tile to your 13, then discard one. Keep going until you have four sets — three in a row (a run) or three the same (a triplet) — and one pair. Winning on someone else’s discard is ron; on your own draw, tsumo.

In Japanese riichi mahjong a win needs at least one yaku (scoring element). When you are one tile from winning without calling, you may declare “riichi”, which is itself a yaku. Red fives (aka dora) and more add to the score.
